Solomon Husher himself commissioned this from Lockwood Fen bog-yew, blackened and half-fossilised by centuries underwater. Here at this desk he wrote his doomy allegory of Winter and its romance with the sun. When he blotted the last word on his manuscript and rose from his work, the timber had turned pale as fresh-cut maple. Or so the story goes.
Something might emerge, if it could only be assured of a hospitable History. Until that time, its dreams might be audible to one who presses an ear against its trembling, sky-scented warmth.
St Januarius is the Name which was wounded; the Name of exceptions; the little god at the door.
Still the best place in the House to get hurt.
Stout, rustic, snug. [Add a Fatigued Soul card to nap, a Maladied soul card to cure it, or (once night has fallen) a Memory to dream on it.]
The Horned-Axe, who opens the way and keeps the threshold, is accounted the last of the Gods-from-Stone.
The Madrugad is the Hour which cannot be unbalanced; which quells and quiets; which comes before the sun.

The Red Grail, birth and appetite, denied and condemned by the clergy of the Sun for her temptress-role in the Sun's division. Those of us who oppose Eternity might instead give her thanks and praise. But cautiously.
The Sun-in-Splendour is the Hour which was sundered; the Hour which is not conquered; the Hour from which proceed all the other Hours of the day. Or so the Church teaches.
The Watchman is the Hour which navigates; which illuminates; which is not compassionate.

The bookwheel is a Dewulf heirloom - a gift to Eva Dewulf from her admirer, the adept Franklin Bancroft. The desk and lectern are much more recent. Steel plaques on both read 'TO GERVINUS VAN LAUREN - IN GRATITUDE FOR HIS ASSISTANCE IN THE CLOSING OF THE WINDING STAIR - E. ABNEY-HASTINGS, NOCTURNAL SECRETARY, 1928'

The prisoners in the Cucurbit were permitted to grow neither too strong, nor too weak. Here they were subjected to an exacting regime which developed both their bodies and their souls, in accordance with the Governor's designs.
The scholars of the House watched the courses of the stars to determine their pasts and understand their future.
The terrible heart of the Governor's terrible project.

Thirza Blake invited a nameless friend (or according to Brancrug tradition, her sister) to Hush House to recover from an illness. Thirza was uncharacteristically secretive about the whole business, perhaps because her own solicitude embarrassed her. She cooked her guest's meals herself; read to her in the afternoons; and purchased this phonograph so her guest could listen to Viennese opera.
This was once strung with yeth-hound gut. Those strings must be long gone, but there's still an unusual savagery to the harp's notes.
Valentine Dewulf put his only friends in cages. Did he close the cage doors?

Where the wild few traffic with the tides.

Fire always accepts gifts. And boils the kettle for tea.
Here I can draw up water - or drop something in, most likely to be lost forever.
Here, the priestesses prepared those meals which they would not, or could not, entrust to their servants.

It's good luck for the villagers to bring little gifts of food to the Librarian. That's already become a tradition. But sometimes the Librarian wants a hot meal, and, these days, the Librarian is the only entity in the house that can cook.
Long ago, this was the route by which provisions entered the gaol, and by which prisoners failed to escape. [Discard objects here, or release beasts.]
Plates, cups and glasses, so that if I want to offer someone wine, I needn't give them the whole bottle.
Since the Conquest, this has been waiting for you. The irreverent might even call it a you tree.

These machines are of different and newer manufacture than the ones above. They include something like a generator, too. But they're in even worse condition. I'll need to provide suitable materials and fuel - and I'll need Scholar-level of Forge to jury-rig them.

Bees, like librarians, are not to be trifled with. Especially these bees. Concealed among their drony bustlings: the elegant worm-curled noble larvae who might one day be the progenitors of the new Blomberende. Blomberende remnants come to pay their respects. [Cuckoo-Honey can sometimes be found in this hive even when it's not Numa.]

The 'Sweet Bones' has been the public house in Brancrug since Cromwell's time. Its history is notable; its beer is not. Guests looking for discreet employment, or for discreet assistance, congregate in the snug.

The Postmistress keeps the gate to the wider world. In her left hand is the lightning (which is to say, the telegraph) and in her right, the thunder (which is to say, the only telephone in Brancrug). Before her lies the cash-register, which accepteth the greater currency and returneth its lesser children.
